Description: Animals are motile in at least one development stage, form from a blastula and gastrula during embryonic development, have collagen, are heterotrophic, and are diploid
Left-right symmetry (sorta)
Anus developes before mouth (contrast protostomia)
Mouth developes before anus (contrast deuterostomia)
Excretory nephridia. If the clade is valid, this includes all bilaterians except Xenaceolomorpha.
Exhibit spiral cleavage, a pattern of early development found in most members of the Lophotrochozoa. (Contrast: radial cleavage).
Includes vertebrates and their relatives. Not all characteristics are present in all life stages.
Anatomy: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, pharyngeal gill slits, post anal tail,  endostyle

Description: Only have a notocord in the larval stage (usually), are also mobile in the larval stage which is often lost in the simple adult form. Lost their myomeric segmentation which other chordates have retained.
Anatomy: Tunic is produced in adults externally of the body, made of a type of cellulose (maybe from horizontal gene transfer).

CommonName: Sea squirts and colonial friends (not actually monophyletic)
Description: Sessile after their larval stage.  Social tunicates retain separate, typical sea squirt bodies, reproduce by stolonous budding, and tend to remain connected by these stolons. They have moderate-sized to small zooids. The zooids of compound ascidians are embedded in a common, colonial tunic.
Anatomy: oral siphon - mouth, leads into pharyngeal basket studded with gill slits. A ventral ridge, the endostyle, forms a seam along the basket, while the dorsal lamina forms a seam along its dorsal margin. The endostyle secrets a mucus net, which is rolled up by the dorsal lamina and passed to the esophagus. The gill slits allow the passage of water through to the atrium exits via the atrial siphon; they are homologous to the gill slits in fishes. Simple gut includes esophagus, small stomach, and long intestine emptying into the atrium. The heart lies on the intestine.

Description: Pelagic for their lifeaspan, solitary and clonial forms. The incurrent and excurrent siphons are 180 degrees apart, thus water flow through the animal becomes a mode of gentle jet propulsion as well.

Colonial zooids share atrial siphon at posterior end. Their name, which means fire body, is derived from their intense bioluminescence, caused by luminescent bacteria that live in a pair of light producing organs on either side of the pharynx.
Complex life cycle with colonial and solitary examples. The bulk of the animal is comprised of a greatly enlarged pharynx and atrium. Viscera is resticted to a small corner of the animal.
Larvaceans retain their chordate features throughout adulthood. They live and filter feed in an house, an external gelatinous casing secreted by the body.
Vertical column to protect the spinal chord, also a cranium to protect the brain. We are vertebrates.
Resemble a filter feeding benthic fish about 1.5–6 cm long.
Anatomy: Dorsal hollow nerve cord and notochord. Buccal cirri surround mouth leading to pharynx with mucus covered gill slits, filted water exits from atrial cavity to atriopore much like a tunicate. Mucus formed at endostyle which lies in the ventral midline of the pharynx catches particles and is passed to digestive cecum.

Description: Names for shared larval structures.
They share some characteristics with chordates, hence their name. A hollow dorsal nerve cord is present in the collar region in some species.
Acorn worms are solitary marine worms
Anatomy: Dorsal nerve cord (not a notocord), gill slits, proboscis, collar, trunk.

Description: Pterobranchs also have a tripartite body plan but look very different. They build tubes and can be social.

Echinoderm means spiny skin. Evolved from bilateral animals, now pentaradial (sorta). Oral-aboral axis instead, but not in sea cucumbers. Larvae are still bilateral. Echinoderms also often have mutable collagenous tissue connecting their ossicles, which can be held ridgid without continued effort (unlike muscles).
Anatomy: Water vascular system, tube feet, madreporite, mesodermal calcitic endoskeleton.

Description: Usually have long arms for suspension feeding coming from central body which is often suspended by the stalk, but unstalked crinoids can swim. Crinoid tube feet lack adhesion discs at the ends but are ciliated to bring food to mouth on the 'top', anus is also on top. Auricularia, doliolaria, vitellaria larvae
Usually predatory marine animals. Many can extend their cardiac stomach onto prey and begin digestion externally. Bipinnaria larvae.
Anatomy: Tube foot, ampulla, madreporite (dorsal), stone canal, ring canal, radial canal, Pedicellaria, pyloric caecum, gonads, stomach (cardiac and pyloric).

Description: The internal organs of digestion and reproduction never enter the arms, as they do in the Asteroidea. Multiple modes of eating, but have only one stomach and have lost their anus. Ophiopluteus larva.
Anatomy: Central disk, madreporite (ventral)

Description: Echinoids have lost their arms, but are still pentaradial (though sand dollars are often offset, and secondarly bilateral again). Echinopluteus larva.
Anatomy: Aristotle's lantern, esophagus, stomach, intestine, gonads, stone canal

Description: Echinoderms that have secondarily evolved bilateral symmetry, have lost their arms. They now have an cylindrical body plan with a anterior and posterior end.
Anatomy: Gonads, tentacles, pharyngeal bulb, stomach, intestine, respiratory tree, cloaca, cloacal sustenders, longitudinal muschles, pollian vessicles, retractor muscles.

Description: Molluscs have a diverse set of physiologies and life histories, leading to their complex taxonomic history. They have a trochophone larve (shared with other trochophorates). Molluscs have a mantle, which secretes a shell in many of the molluscan groups.
Anatomy: Ventral muscular foot, Radula (teeth), Mantle (epithelial structure that secretes the shell)

Description: Deep sea worms that secrete calcareous spicules instead of a shell
Deep sea benthic animals with a single shell, thought to be extinct until 1950s. Not to be confused with gastropod limpets.
Generally shallow, intertidal
Anatomy: Seven or eight separate shell plates, girdle (edge of mantle, often embedded with spicules)

Description: Torsion rotates the visceral mass so the anus is above the head
Most intellegent invertebrates, tentacles (suckers on end) or arms (suckers whole way down)
Anatomy: Closed circulatory system, Foot modified into the siphon and arms/tentacles, Shell that is reduced or lost (usually), Large collection of cerebral ganglia

Description: Still have their shell, used to be much more diverse
Anatomy: External coiled/chambered shell

Description: Reduced internal shell, Chromatophores - pigmented cells that produce color, contraction and expansion of sacs allow color change
Anatomy: Arms vs tentacles (foot), siphon, beak, mouth, mantle, heart, gills, heart

Description: Laterally compressed between two valves (shells), usually sessile
Anatomy: Anterior and posterior adductor muscles, gills, incurrent and excurrent siphon, palial line, palial siphon, umbo, hinge teeth, byssal threads, mantle, foot, gut, heart

Description: True metameric segmenation and often chitinous cheatae
Polycheate means 'many bristles', and they usually do have many brisltes.
Anatomy: Parapodia (incl. Notopodia, neuropodia, cheatae), prostomium, antennae, peristomium, anal cirrus

Description: have a collar / clitellum - the thicker girdle that is used to secrete the casing for their eggs
All individuals are hermaphroditic
Anatomy: Clitellum, pharynx, hearts, seminal vessicles, crop, gizzard, intenstines, dorsal blood vessel, nephridia

Description: Most feed on blood or hemolymph, few concume prey whole. Leaches have suckers to attach to hosts and move around. Cheatae are lost secondarily.
Unsegmented, usually predators or parasites
Anatomy: Rhynchocoel - proboscis with stylet in fluid filled cavity

Description: Unsegmented, blind gut, cute eye spots but no respiratory or circulatory systems. Often aquatic or parasitic.
Generally endoparasites
Anatomy: Gravid proglottids - egg-filled segments easily released

Description: Most are free-living, aquatic terrestrial or marine. Includes planarians
Internal parasites with complex life cycles. Different life stages infect different animals, cerceria cause swimmers itch and schistasomiasis.
Cute and small, increadibly resilient
Many legs, prey on other inverts by shooting adhesive slime from oral papillae which is suched back into the gut by a muscular pharynx. 13-25 pairs of legs (lobopods)
Jointed legs, chitinous exoskeleton
Centepedes, millipedes and friends. Many legs.
One pair of legs per segment
Two pairs of legs per segment

Spiders and Friends. The chelicerate body plan generally consists of two tagmata, the prosoma and the opisthosoma. The chelicerae, are the only appendages before the mouth. Chelicerae are generally modest pincers used to feed. However, spiders' chelicerae form fangs that most species use to inject venom into prey.
Not crabs, only living example is horseshoe crabs.
Not spiders, marine animals.
Eight legs on cephalothorax, also chelicera and pedipalps
These air-breathing arthropods that have eight limbs, chelicerae with fangs generally able to inject venom, and spinnerets that extrude silk.
No stinger, but can spray acetic acid
If you have heard the myth that they are very venomous but their fangs are too small to puncture skin, that is not true at all.
Extinct ancesteral arthropod
Anatomy: Cephalon, Thorax, Pygidium

Description: Six legs
Anatomy: Three body sections. Head: acron + 5 segments, Thorax: 3 segments, Abdomen: 11 segments

CommonName: AKA Entognatha. Springtails, diplurans and proturans
Description: Six legs but wingless. Entognatha refers to refers to morphology of mouth - mandibles and maxillae are housed in a gnathal pouch
Six legs, three part body plan (head, thorax, abdomen), antennae. Most diverse group of animals.
The ovipositor is often modified into a stinger in these insects (hence, males don't sting). Generally well developed mandibles and four winds held together with hamuli. Can be social or solitary.
Most diverse group of animals
These are the true bugs. The name derives from half-wing, because the forewing is often leathery at the base, but membranous at the tips.

Predatory flying insects, with voracious aquatic larvae as well. Dragonflys have larger eyes which wrap around much of the head and wings that remain down when resting. Damselflies are generally more slender, have lateral eyes and close the wings when resting.
These insects have coloured scales overing the body, triangular wings, and a proboscis to drink water. Larvae (caterpillars) are come from eggs generally laid on a host plant.
Single front set of wings (hense name), hindwings evolved into halteres, organs that sense rotation to coordinate flight.

Produce sound by stridulation, rubbing the wings on legs or eachother. Incomplete metamorphosis. Generally well developed hind legs for jumping, and flying hindwings that fold under the tegmina (hardened forewings) at rest.
Termites are often eusocial insects, and cockroaches have been considered pre-social in some aggrigating species. Many behavioural similarites between the groups.
Segmented animals with a common body plan of 20 body segments (rarely 21) divided into a head, thorax, and abdomen.

CommonName: Rolly-pollies, wood lice, giant deep sea isopods
Description: Branching appendages on the abdomen that are used in respiration. Females brood their young in a pouch under their thorax. Inabit a diversity of marine, freshwater, and terrestrial species with diverse diets.

Crustaceans that generally have a laterally compressed body and no carapace. Gills are located on the legs and the head is fused to the thorax. Many marine species but also freshwater and terrestrial species.

Krill are small and exclusively marine crustaceas with a clear carapace (generally). An important food source for many larger animals. Technically there are no walking legs, but there is 5 sets of swimming legs.
Crazy animals, can see more colours than us, and can punch hard enough to break shells.

Crustaceans with ten periopods (walking legs) on the last 5 thoracic segments, the first ones often end in chelae. Many are are scavengers. Only ten periopods, but they can have as many as 38 appendages.
Carideans typically have two pairs of chelae and include many marine and freshwater species. Commercially important animals.
Anatomy: Stalked eyes, carapace

Description: These decapods have chelae on each of the first three pairs of pereiopods. Include many marine and freshwater species
Anatomy: Gastric muscles, mandibular muscles, gills, cardiac stomach, pyloric stomach, digestive glands, intestine, testes, heart, antennal gland.

Description: These decapods lack chelae, hense the name. Enlarged second antennae and phyllosoma larvae.
Many instances of carcinisation here. The last pair of legs is often reduced so a "crab" with only eight visible legs is generally an anomuran.
True crabs with ten visible legs, the first ones end in chelae. Abdomen is often small and tucked under the thorax.

CommonName: Brine shrimp, triops, water fleas, etc
Description: United by the presence of gills on many of the animals' appendages, hense the name. Carapace in many forms, and generally have compound eyes.

These crustaceans have a bivalve-like shell that hinges on the top, made of chitin and sometimes calcium carbonate. Very abundant in the vossil record, though extant species especially are generally quite small.
Small and abundant crustaceans. Most copepods have a single median bright-red compound eye.
Parastic crustaceans. The name means 'five-openings', whish isn't true. There is one mouth with appendages and the rest of the appendages are hooks to hold onto hosts.
Highly derived group of sessile arthropods. Most are suspension feeders - feed with cirri.
Diploblastic: have an ectoderm, endoderm and a mesoglea. All have stinging cells called Nematocytes (cnidocytes), which contain a nematocyst (cnida). Blind gut and no circulatory system.
Have a true medusa stage
Many have a colonial polyp stage and planktonic medusae stage. Includes siphonophores, such as Portuguese man o’ war, where polyps have division of jobs.
Medusae have no velum. Asexual stage where medusae will bud off a polyp - strobilation.
Polyp and medusae stage. Distinctive 4 sides. A few species have deadly stings. More complex nervous system with complex eyes and a ring nerve.
Attached medusoid form. Do not have a polyp phase
Sea anemones, stony corals, soft corrals and sea pens. Generally sessile as adults.
Six fold symmetry
Typically sessile, some have symbiotic relationships with zooxanthellae or dinoflagellates
Secrete calcium carbonate -- built key habitat of the ocean’s most diverse regions. Many are colonial but can also be solitary. Many have symbionts called zooxanthellae.
Generally deep sea. Characteristic thin, flexible black skeleton. Affected by poaching.
Solitary polyps without skeletons

CommonName: Generally colonial polyps, attached by a string-like structure called a stolon, or arranged in mats but can be solitary. Soft structure - commonly incorporate sand and other material for structure.

Description: Eight fold symmetry

CommonName: Soft corals and gorgonians, see fans
Description: Many are soft with skeletal elements called sclerites, but gorgonians make a hard skeleton. Found all over - many thrive in nutrient rich water, unlike stony corals.
Colonial polyps. Primary polyp off of which the other polyps grow (rather than mineralized skeleton).
Forms a crystalline calcareous skeleton - unlike other octocorals. Generally a blueish color.
Aquatic simple animals. no true tissues
Calcium carbonate spicules. Generally small animals.
Spicules made of spongin, silicate, or calcium carbonate. Most diverse sponges.
Four- and/or six-pointed siliceous spicules. Found in deep sea - estimated to live up to 15,000 years.
No stinging cells, but have sticky coloblast cells. Some have transient anus. Recently thought to be sister to all other animals but that is contentious.
Anatomy: Ctene (fused ciliary plates) arranged in rows (look like combs). Mouth and gastrovascular canals, some lead to an anus. Apical sense organ.

Description: Ctenophores in this class have no tentacles
These cenophores have long, contractile tentacles that can retract into specialized sheaths.

Ubiquitous in nature, nematodes account for about 80% of all individual animals. Huge size range. Many are parasites, including Ascaris, one of the most common parasitic infections in humans worldwide. Cuticle is formed mostly of protiens, not the polysaccharide chitin.
Anatomy: Intestine, vagina, uterus, oviducts.

Description: Top and bottom valve hinged at the rear end, unlike molluscan bivalves with left-right valves. Formed from the Ancient Greek words brachion ("arm") and podos ("foot").
Crabs but also bugs
These animals have a chitin based (usually) exoskeleton which they shed to grow (ecdysis).
Have either a trochophote larvae stage or a lophophore.
Small, usually solitary, 'wheels' of cilia - the corona.
Predatory marine worms, hooks on each side of the mouth
Parasitic in arthropods, hard external cuticle
Simple flattened worms, most basal bilaterians
True tissues, organized body plans, and differetiated systems.
Small, live in sedentary colonies, single animals called zooids
Unsegmented worms, extensible spiny proboscis.
Simplest of animals, move with ciliary motion. Not discovered until 1883, and still only three species described.
